H1.text: Every equation you have solved so far had an answer you could point to on the number line.

H2.text: x minus three equals zero? Point at three. x squared equals four? Point at two, or minus two.

H3.text: Last night, Aarav met one that broke the rule. A new chapter begins with it.

H4.text: x squared plus one equals zero. He tried every number he could think of. Not one of them worked.

H5.text: Is the equation broken, or is our number line too small? Let us find out.

P1.text: So why does no number work?

P2.text: Look at what squaring does. Three squared is nine. Minus three squared is also nine, because minus times minus is plus.

P3.text: Zero squared is zero. A square can be zero or positive, but never negative.

P4.text: Watch it live. As x slides along the number line, x squared never drops below zero.

P5.text: So x squared plus one is always at least one. It can never reach zero.

L1.text: Now the big picture. Draw the graph of y equals x squared plus c, where c is a number we can change.

L2.text: Where the curve crosses the x axis, y is zero. So the crossing points are the real solutions.

L3.text: Start with c equal to minus four. The curve cuts the axis at two and at minus two.

L4.text: Now let c count up. At minus one, the crossings move in, to one and minus one.

L5.text: At c equal to zero, the curve just touches the axis, at one point.

L6.text: And the moment c passes zero, the curve lifts off. No crossing at all. No real solution.

L7.text: At c equal to one, we reach our equation. The curve floats one full unit above the axis.

D1.text: Let us prove it in four small steps.

D2.text: Step one. Start with x squared plus one equals zero.

D3.text: Step two. Subtract one from both sides. x squared equals minus one.

D4.text: Step three. But for every real number x, x squared is zero or more. We just watched that.

D5.text: Step four. A number cannot be zero or more, and also equal minus one. So no real number solves it.

S1.text: Side by side. x squared minus one equals zero. The curve dips below the axis and crosses it twice, at one and minus one.

S2.text: x squared plus one equals zero. The curve stays above the axis. It never crosses, so there is no real solution.

S3.text: Now you try. Does x squared plus four equals zero have a real solution? Pause and decide.

S4.text: No! x squared is never negative, so x squared plus four is at least four. It can never reach zero.

Z1.text: This is not the first time numbers ran out.

Z2.text: With only counting numbers, x plus five equals two has no answer. So we added zero and the negatives.

Z3.text: Two x equals three has no integer answer. So we added fractions.

Z4.text: x squared equals two has no fraction answer. So we added root two, and got the real numbers.

Z5.text: Each time an equation got stuck, the number system grew. Now x squared equals minus one is stuck again.

Z6.text: People saw this long ago. The Indian mathematicians Mahavira and Bhaskara wrote that a negative number has no square root.

Z7.text: In fifteen forty five, Cardan looked for two numbers that add to ten and multiply to forty. He got five plus root minus fifteen, and called such answers useless.

I1.text: So mathematicians did what they did before. They made the number system bigger.

I2.text: They named a new number, i, whose square is minus one. In symbols, i is the square root of minus one.

I3.text: Now x equals i solves our equation. i squared plus one is minus one plus one, which is zero.

T1.text: Remember this. No real number has a negative square. That is why we need a new kind of number.

U1.text: But where does i live? Not on the number line. Here is the clever part.

U2.text: Multiplying by minus one flips a number to the other side. Three becomes minus three. That is a half turn.

U3.text: And i times i is minus one. So multiplying by i, done twice, must make a half turn.

U4.text: Two equal moves that make a half turn are two quarter turns. So multiplying by i turns a number a quarter turn, off the line, straight up.

U5.text: The new numbers need a second direction. That is why they are called complex numbers.

U6.text: Quick one. Start at three and multiply by i twice. Where do you land? Pause and think.

U7.text: Minus three! Two quarter turns make a half turn. Three times i squared is three times minus one.

W2.text: Show that x squared plus four x plus five equals zero has no real solution. Then solve it using i.

W3.text: Step one. Split five into four plus one, and group the first three terms.

W4.text: Step two. x squared plus four x plus four is x plus two, all squared. So x plus two, squared, equals minus one.

W5.text: Step three. A real square cannot be negative, so there is no real solution.

W6.text: Step four. With i, x plus two can be i, or minus i. So x is minus two plus i, or minus two minus i.

W7.text: The graph agrees. Its lowest point sits at height one, so the curve never touches the axis.

X2.text: Many students say minus one solves x squared equals minus one, because minus one squared looks like minus one.

X3.text: But minus one, in brackets, squared, is minus one times minus one. That is plus one. So minus one is not a solution.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In PUC board exams, from this NCERT chapter. A typical question: show that an equation has no real solution, then solve it with i.

Q1.text: Exam level now. For how many integers c does this equation have no real solution? Pause and solve.

A2.text: Complete the square. x minus two, squared, equals four minus c.

A3.text: A real square is never negative. So there is no real solution exactly when four minus c is negative, that is, when c is more than four.

A4.text: At c equal to four, x equals two still works. So c runs from five to twenty. That is sixteen integers.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does x squared plus nine equals zero have no real solution?

Y3.text: Two. For which values of c does the graph of y equals x squared plus c miss the x axis?

Y4.text: Three. Is minus one, in brackets, squared, equal to minus one?

N1.text: Next time: i times i is minus one. So what is i times i times i? The powers of i repeat every four turns.
